1.reasoning: The Nigerian CRS syllabus treats God's sovereignty in creation through the creation of man, made in God's image and given dominion over all other creatures (Gen 1:26-28), which is the one option that expresses sovereignty rather than simply being a created thing. The strongest case against B is a chronological reading of 'first', since waters and animals come before man. That reading does not settle on one letter, though: rivers are not a distinct act in Gen 1 and appear only incidentally in Gen 2:10, and animals come after the waters, so it cannot be what the setter meant. Eve is part of the creation of mankind and comes after the man, so B is the answer an examiner would accept.

10.reasoning: Jeremiah warned Judah of judgement and punishment for its idolatry and unfaithfulness, and also gave hope of return from exile and a new covenant (Jer 29:10-14; 31:31-34). This double message is the standard textbook description of his prophecy. Law and order, wealth and prosperity, and dreams and visions do not describe his message; the last is the only one with any pull, because prophets received revelations, but that is how a message comes and not what it says. B is the only defensible option.

13.reasoning: At Babel God confused the language of all humanity and scattered them over the face of the earth (Gen 11:1-9). This is the standard syllabus illustration of God's sovereignty over the nations as a whole. The strongest rival is B, because choosing Israel also shows sovereign choice, but it is God's election of one people rather than his rule over the nations. Manna and the parting of the Jordan are provision and miracles for Israel alone. A is the clear key.

20.reasoning: Jer 24:1 and 29:1-2 place Jeremiah in Jerusalem when Nebuchadnezzar carried Jehoiachin (Jeconiah) into exile in 597 BC, and Jeremiah wrote to those exiles. Ezekiel would be the stronger answer, since he went into exile with the king, but he is not among the options. Elijah and Hosea prophesied centuries earlier and Malachi after the exile, so none of them could have witnessed it. A is the only chronologically possible answer.

28.reasoning: The Sadducees are identified throughout the Gospels and Acts by their denial of the resurrection (Matt 22:23; Mark 12:18; Acts 23:8), and this is the doctrine Nigerian CRS texts attach to them. The strongest case for A is that Acts 23:8 also says they denied angels and spirits. However, the stem asks for 'the doctrine', and the resurrection is the defining, repeatedly cited denial that examiners test; angels comes up only in that one verse, as an addition. Prophecy and the Law of Moses are wrong, because the Sadducees upheld the Torah. C is the key an examiner would mark.

33.reasoning: The instruction to 'clothe yourselves with humility' is tied to the reason 'God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble' (1 Pet 5:5, quoting Prov 3:34; cf. Jas 4:6). Paul uses the clothing image for humility in Col 3:12. The stem's attribution to Paul's letters is loose, but the error does not make any other option more defensible. Material riches, Jewish tradition and political power are not reasons the New Testament gives for humility. A is unambiguous.

36.reasoning: The stem is badly worded and options B and D are both printed as 'children', but the intended meaning, 'whom did Peter urge to endure (unjust suffering)', can still be recovered. In 1 Pet 2:18-20 Peter tells servants (slaves) to submit to their masters and endure unjust suffering patiently, which is the passage this item tests. The best argument for A is that wives are also told to submit in 1 Pet 3:1-6, but that passage is about winning unbelieving husbands by conduct, not enduring suffering. The duplicated distractor is a typesetting fault that does not affect the key, so this is not defective.
